outline_section.section_title: Introduction to Definition of Continuous-Time Convolution
outline_section.learning_goal: Define continuous-time convolution as the LTI output formed by integrating weighted, shifted impulse responses over all input times.

image_policy.image_description_seed: A clean LTI-system diagram showing x(t) decomposed into weighted impulses x(tau)d tau, each producing a shifted impulse response h(t-tau), with all contributions accumulating into y(t).
visual_elements: LTI system block labeled impulse response h(t)
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Use a simple signal-processing block diagram that reduces cognitive load; avoid numerical signal plots, dense annotations, and decorative imagery.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: State the convolution integral and identify it as the LTI output produced by adding the responses to all weighted impulse components of the input.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a generic LTI system with input x(t), impulse response h(t), and output y(t), without evaluating the integral.
paragraph_plan: Connect to the prior idea that a continuous-time input can be represented as an accumulation of weighted impulses.
Explain that an impulse located at time tau produces a shifted impulse response, and its weight comes from the input value at that time.
State that adding all infinitesimal shifted responses over tau gives the output at time t.
Introduce convolution notation y(t)=(x*h)(t) and the integral definition.
Clarify that this lesson is about formulating and interpreting the definition, not computing convolution values or overlap intervals.
display_math_plan: Optionally show the phrase output = accumulation of weighted shifted impulse responses next to the formula.

outline_section.handoff_notes: Keep this as minimum-effective-dose direct instruction. Do not introduce flip-shift-multiply mechanics, overlap-area reasoning, or integral-bound computation.
